Mühlradt, Aus Konitz’ vergangenen Chojnice (German: Konitz) is a town situated in the area of the Krajna Lake District dominated by moraine hills (130–140 masl) and numerous lakes. This town established in the 14th century was located between two lakes – Zakonne Lake (Mönchsee) from the south and Cegielniane Lake (Ziegelsee) from the north and east. The stream called jarcewo Stream, formerly known as Chojnica, flowed into Charzykowy Lake situated 7 km north of jarcewska Stream1. The oldest signs of settlement near the town date back to the New Stone Age – the Neolithic Era (4200–1700 BC), but its development did not become intense until the period of the Lusatian culture (1300–400 BC). In the original stage of the Iron Age, peoples of the Pomeranian culture settled in the area of the future county of Chojnice, the evidence of which are characteristic cist graves and a settlement in Odry (40 km north-west of Chojnice). The cooling of the climate and increasing precipitation which started at the end of the 3rd century BC deterioratedliving conditions and caused a prolonged crisis in the settlement which lasted almost three centuries. It was not until the arrival of the Goths from Scandinavia that the settlement in the vicinity of Chojnice was revived. The best preserved and examined evidence of the Goths’ stay are extensive cemeteries of the 1st– –3rd centuries AD in Odry and Leśno (30 km north of Chojnice). Archeological finds from the period confirm the existence of trade contacts with the Roman Empire (Pawłowo, 4 km south of Chojnice)2. The emigration of the Goths which began in the 4th century caused a settlement reduction interrupted in the 7th century by the influx of Slavic peoples. Undoubtedly, in the period between the mid-7th and the 10th centuries the settlement developed in the areas situated in the vicinity of Chojnice. On the south-western coast of Charzykowy Lake (4 km north-west) and Obrowo (15 km south-east of Chojnice) archeological research revealed the remains of gords (Slavic burgwalls), while on the eastern coast of Ostrowite Lake (6 km north-east of Chojnice) an open settlement existed from the 9th to the 11th century3.

In the last quarter of the 10th century Gdańsk Pomerania (Pomeralia) was conquered by Prince Mieszko I and incorporated into the Piast monarchy. Some of the burgwalls were destroyed whilst other gords lost their importance. In the system of royal administration the main role was played by gords resided by castellans. The area of the future town was located between local authority centres in Raciąż (at present the village of Mrowiniec 14 km east) and in Szczytno (24 km west)4. The results of the archeological examination do not confirm the hypothesis about the existence of a castellan gord in Chojnice. In the years 1034–1038 Pomeranian tribes toppled the Piast rule and maintained control until Bolesław III Wrymouth conquered the area again after prolonged fighting (1115–1119). During the period of the Piast rule in Gdańsk Pomerania there were created a few centres managed by governors who came from the local Pomeranian oligarchy and were appointed by the dukes of Cracow. At the end of the 12th century, Chojnice Land constituted part of the Lubiszewo-Świecie territory managed by the governor Grzymisław5. At the beginning of the 13th century the area was taken over by dukes of Gdańsk who wanted to become independent from Poland. According to the treaty concluded in 1282 after the death of the duke Mściwój II of Gdańsk, the territory was taken over by the duke Przemysław II of Greater Poland and incorporated into the revived Kingdom of Poland in 12956. The next change in the territorial rule of Chojnice was connected with the expansion of the Teutonic Order, which conquered Gdańsk Pomerania (Pomerelia) and incorporated it to the State of the Teutonic Order in Prussia in 13097. The first source record about Chojnice appears in two documents of 1275 which mention a knight Myślibor Malowy de Choyniz8 as a witness of the description of the borders of the monastery of St. Augustine situated at Charzykowy Lake. It is very probable that the information referred to a village later on known as jarcewo, located 6 km north of the place between Zakonne Lake and Cegielniane Lake9. It is possible that at the end of the 13th century settlers started to arrive in the territory of the future town; nevertheless, the thesis about Pomeranian dukes establishing there a settlement and granting it a town charter10 has not been confirmed in either written or archeological sources11. The creation of the town of Chojnice is connected with the formation of the Teutonic Order’s territorial rule which began in the second decade of the 14th century after the area had been conquered by the Teutonic Knights. The most important elements of the process were the creation of the structures of territorial administration and

the development of settlement. Between 1312 and 1320 the commandry of Człuchów (Schlochau) was set up, the borders of which included the south-western part of Gdańsk Pomerania12. As the foundation charter did not survive, the exact date and conditions of the town’s foundation are unknown. The town must have existed as early as 1323, for an entry from 1323 mentions Reinhard, the vogt (reeve) of Chojnice and two burghers – Friczko and johannes Saxo13. Probably the decision to establish the town was taken in the middle of the second decade of the 14th century and was connected with the Teutonic Order’s plans to colonise rural areas in the immediate vicinity of the town14. It was then that the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order Karl von Trier granted four villages (Kładow [Kladau], Krojanty [Krojanten], Wielki Zbenin [Groβ Zbenin] and Mały Zbenin [Klein Zbenin]) situated north-west of the town to new settlers obliging them to serve him as knights15. Within the next twenty years a well-developed settlement structure was formed, which consisted of villages and estates obliged to serve as knights. In 1323 and 1326 with the permission of the Grand Master, the commander of Człuchów granted two privileges to manors in Moszczenica (Mosnitz) and the villages of Chojniczki (Klein Konitz) and Nowa Cerkiew (Neukirch). Privileges granted to manors in Klawkowy (Grunsberg), Pawłowek (Pagelkau) and the villages of Rychnowy (Richnau) and Brzezno (Briesen) date back to the 1340s. 16 Transport conditions were one of the factors which determined the choice of the site to establish the town. The place situated between lakes was crossed by a route connecting Pomerelia with the West; it was not particularly significant, but it started to play a fundamental role in the communication between the Monastic State and the Reich after the residence of the Grand Master had been relocated to Malbork (Marienburg) (1309). Chojnice was crossed by routes leading north to Gdańsk and Słupsk (Stolp), and south in the direction of Tuchola (Tuchel), but these were secondary trade routes17. Chojnice played a significant role in developing the underpopulated south-eastern border of Pomerelia, which is why it was granted extensive estates by the Teutonic Order at the moment of the town’s foundation18. In 1346 the Grand Master Heinrich Dusemer granted Chojnice burghers some additional 31 lans of the forest which extended south-west of Charzykowy Lake. In the renewed foundation privilege of 1360 the Grand Master Winrich von Kniprode confirmed the act of granting the town 125 lans, twenty-five of which were exempt from rent, whilst the remaining 100 lans were charged with a rent of one goose and 10 bushels of grain19. Owners of plots situated in the town were made to pay a small tax of 6 dinars in the way of the recognition of the Teutonic Order’s supremacy. Apart from the land tax, the municipality was obliged to make annual payments of 30 marks to the commander in Człuchów and provide him with 12 pounds of pepper and 4 barrels of tallow in exchange for using fair facilities in the market. The Grand Master allowed burghers to fish in two lakes (Zielone Lake and jeleńcz Lake) situated deep inside the Tuchola Forest (17 km north of the town) and granted them the usufruct of two water mills. Burghers were also granted the Grand Master’s privilege of 1377 which allowed them to construct two windmills in the area exempt from rent, which contributed to the development of the milling industry in Chojnice. The grant of the mills was exceptional in the Monastic State as the Teutonic Order was generally reluctant to give their subjects privileges resulting from the milling royal rights20.

In the privilege of 1360 the Grand Master confirmed the granting of the Kulm Law to the town, which defined the legal-political rules and the organisation of the town’s authorities21. In the original stage of the town’s development the judicial and administrative power belonged to the hereditary head of a municipality – hereditary mayor [Schultheiß] recorded in 1323 and 1326, appointed by the territorial ruler. The entry in the foundation privilege according to which the town was given one-third of the revenue from fines imposed by lower courts indicates that before 1360 the town council managed to take over the mayor’s office. It is possible that the municipality took over the office of the hereditary mayor prior to 1346, for the privilege granting the forest to the town mentions only burghers of Chojnice22. At that time the council became the most important body of the city’s administration. A mayor as the head of the town council appears in the records for the first time in 1366. According to the information from the 1430s and 1440s, the council originally consisted of the mayor, the mayor’s deputy, the treasury administrator and his deputy, and four town councillors. The town council was responsible for administering the municipality’s wealth, representing it to the territorial ruler, and guaranteeing safety and order in the town. With the permission of the territorial ruler the council could also pass statutes (Willkür) which regulated the organisation of city life23. The second body of the local authority was the judicial bench, first recorded in 1448, headed by a judge elected from the members of the bench. According to the foundation privilege, the municipal court’s competence included only the so-called lower jurisdiction, whilst criminal offences were dealt with by the commander of Człuchów. Burghers had the right to elect a mayor, town councillors and members of the court bench, but their choice had to be accepted by the Teutonic Order. Representatives of four most important guilds (clothiers, smiths, butchers, bakers) who composed the board referred to as “vierwerken“ participated in making decisions concerning all the inhabitants of the town. Chojnice was the most important city in the Człuchów commandry, the evidence of which was the fact that in 1360 the Grand Master established there land tribunals for the knighthood. In the first half of the 15th century in Chojnice local conventions of the knighthood took place24. After Chojnice had been incorporated into the Polish Kingdom, basic elements of the city’s political system were maintained. Privileges granted by Polish kings boosted the role of the local authorities. On the strength of the privilege granted by Casimirus IV jagiellon to Prussian towns in 1454, the town council had the right to pass city statutes (Willkür). The privilege granted by Sigismund III Vasa of 1593 extended the judicial authority of the council in the city and the city’s land estates. In the period from the 16th to the 18th centuries the council consisted of 9–10 members who were elected from among the most affluent burghers, mainly merchants and people with university education. From 1555 only Protestants were allowed to be members of the council. The head of the council was the presiding mayor assisted by his two deputies, the vice-mayor and the third mayor (since 1629). The second mayor was responsible for the administration of the municipal forest, while the third mayor dealt with education and was the head of the orphans’ court25. Officials appointed from among the councilmen were responsible for various areas of city life. New councilmen were elected and appointed to various offices in the council every year at an election meeting called “Kühre”. Decisions made at the meeting were approved in the name of the king by the starost of Człuchów26. Like in the Middle Ages, the treasury administrator (Kämmerer) and his deputy were in charge of the city’s budget. The excise and milling councilman (Akzise-Mühlen Herr) collected alcohol excise tax and tax from the revenues of mills. Committees consisting of members of the council were appointed to administer land estates (Korn und Feld Herr), the municipal forest (Wald-Herr) and cases concerning the construction industry in the city (Bauherr). Offices connected with the economic activity of the city council included the office managing coach-houses and brickworks (Podwoden und Ziegelscheune Inspektion). A fire councilor monitored the observance of fire regulations and supervised all night watchmen. One of the councillors performed the function of judge and presided over the court bench. From among members of the council board there were elected officials supervising Protestant churches (Kirchen Direktion) and city schools (Protoscholar and Scholarcha). To make the judicial work more efficient in the first half of the 18th century, two new judicial offices were created: the orphans’ court (1727) dealing with the division and guardianship of the property of minors, and the court of commerce (Wettegericht) (1744) set up to examine cases concerning offences against regulations of city statutes. Administrative councillors were supported by over a dozen assistants employed by the council, among whom the most important position was held by a city notary who was required to have university education and knowledge of the Chelmno law as well as a command of three languages – Latin, German and Polish27.

The court’s bench consisted of a judge and 11 aldermen elected for life from among the craftsmen. Like in other cities of Royal Prussia, in the second half of the 16th century in Chojnice, a new body of the local authority was established – the so called third estate – the responsibility of which was to represent all citizens, monitor the city’s finances and codecide with the city council about the most important issues concerning the city. From among members of the third estate there were appointed three representatives to the court of commerce (Wettegericht) and members of the body looking after the poor ( since 1755)28. After the Polish-Lithuanian army defeated the army of the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order in the battle of Grunwald on 15 july 1410, the inhabitants of Chojnice refused to recognise the Polish king, unlike the inhabitants of most towns of the Teutonic State. The town and the castle in Człuchów played a very important role as stage stations for mercenaries arriving from the German Reich to help the Teutonic Order in Prussia29. Wars between Poland-Lithuania and the Teutonic Order in the second and third decade of the 15th century took place mainly in territories situated on the right river bank of the Vistula. It was not until the war of 1431–1435 that Chojnice played a major role as an important defence point on the way from the New March and Greater Poland to the Monastic State. In july and August 1433, the city was unsuccessfully besieged by the Polish army supported by the Husite military units30. In the Monastic State of the Teutonic Order in Prussia, small towns did not participate actively in political life until the beginning of the 15th century. Only representatives of big cities and the knighthood were invited to conventions with the Grand Master. It was the lost war with Poland-Lithuania (1409-11) and a growing crisis of the structures of the territorial rule in the first half of the 15th century that caused the increasing political activity of small towns. Representatives of Chojnice participated only in 4 conventions. The city also played the role of a guarantor of the peace treaty concluded between the Teutonic Order and Poland-Lithuania in 1422. In a political conflict between the Teutonic Order and the Prussian estates the council of Chojnice supported the territorial ruler. Despite the fact that the city’s stamp was sealed to the foundation document of the Prussian Confederation in 1440, in 1446 the council of Chojnice took the side of the Grand Master, and in 1450 together with the councils of Toruń and Malbork it withdrew from the Prussian Confederation31. The outbreak of the uprising of the Prussian estates against the Teutonic Order on 6 February 1454 entailed a change in the political stand of burghers of Chojnice, who on 15 February overthrew the council; the new authorities forsook their allegiance to the commander of Człuchów. The town deprived of the military support of the Prussian Confederation could not resist the attack of mercenaries from the Reich. From the end of March 1454 Chojnice became the most important defence point of the Teutonic Order in Pomerelia32. The Polish army and military units of the Prussian Confederation besieged the city unsuccessfully from April 1454. On 18 September 1454 in the battle of Chojnice, the Teutonic army defeated the armies of the Polish king and the Prussian Confederation, which had an enormous influence on the course of the war33. For another 12 years the person who in fact had the power over the city was Kacper Nostyc, the commander of the mercenaries serving the Grand Master. It was not until the siege of july 1466 during which most of the city was destroyed that the mercenaries were forced to surrender on 28 September. The Second Peace of Toruń concluded on 19 October 1466 terminated the long war; on the strength of the treaty Pomerelia – as Royal Prussia – was incorporated into the Polish Kingdom34.

In the new political and territorial structure the former commandry of Człuchów, where Chojnice was situated, was turned into a district. A starost resided in the castle in Człuchów; he administered all royal estates and represented the royal authority to burghers and peasants. Nevertheless, it was Chojnice that played the role of the political centre in the Człuchów district; in the town there took place conventions of the nobility from the district and sessions of land tribunals35. The council of Chojnice sent its delegates to the assemblies of the general dietine of Royal Prussia. It also played an active role in the association of small towns established in 1662, the responsibility of which was to protect their interests against the nobility and the abuse of royal officials. In the association Chojnice represented also adjacent smaller towns such as Biały Bór, Człuchowa, Czarne, Debrzno and Tuchola36. When the last military conflict between Poland and the Teutonic Order ended in 1525, Royal Prussia enjoyed over 100 years of peace interrupted in the first half of the 17th century by the war with Sweden. During the first invasion of Swedes in Pomerelia in the years 1626–1629 Chojnice remained on the sidelines of military activities. However, the city was heavily affected by the war of 1655–1660. In September 1655 Chojnice was conquered by King Charles X Gustav; during the conflict, the suburbs were burnt down and burghers were forced to pay contributions and accommodate Swedish soldiers. The Polish troops made several attempts to regain the city from April 1656. They managed to do so in September 1656, but during the fighting, the suburbs were ruined again. In january 1657 the Swedish army marched into the city after a three-day siege. During the fights buildings in Chojnice were heavily affected. The damage was aggravated by the epidemic and great fire which destroyed the city in December 1657. In the autumn of 1657 the Swedes withdrew from most smaller towns of Pomerelia; nevertheless, in February 1659 the Swedish army units plundered Chojnice again. The treaty concluded in Oliwa in 1660 concluded the war, but the effects of it hindered the development of the city for many years. As a result of the military campaigns, most buildings in the city were destroyed, the population declined, and the city’s treasury had a debt of 80,000 florins. The Great Northern War (1701–1721) entailed more damage and poverty in the city. Chojnice was forced to accommodate soldiers and pay contributions to the Saxon, Swedish and Russian armies. The plundering of the city by the army of the tsar Peter I in 1706 bore especially painful effects. The mayor Isaak Gottfried estimated the losses borne by the city during the war at 200,000 florins. The economic crisis of the city became even more serious during the Seven year War (1756–1763) when the Russian army marching to Brandenburg through Royal Prussia forced burghers to accommodate soldiers and to provide them victuals37.

The city plan of Chojnice shows the typical layout of a small town in the Monastic State of the Teutonic Order in Prussia – a regular square shape measuring 300m2 with a centrally located market. The irregular line of the city’s frontier in the south-east part was determined by landform features. Among small Prussian towns with an average surface of 6.5 hectares, Chojnice with its surface of about 9 hectares constituted one of the biggest centres. Originally two strips of blocks consisting of burghers’ plots were allotted around the market of 70x80 m. The block between the city walls and the eastern block adjoining the market was designed for the construction of a parish church. The quick development of the city meant that in the second half of the 14th century the areas situated at Cegielniane Lake were incorporated into the city’s juristiction38. A new district was named “New Town”. Probably in the beginning the city area was divided into 180 plots; as a result of the city’s expansion, another 70 plots were created. The oldest information about the number of houses and plots come from the 16th century. The illustration of 1565 mentions 250 houses situated within the city walls. Meanwhile, in the description of the city of 1570 there appears information about 223 houses, thirty-nine of which were located at the market, one hundred forty-nine in the streets and fifty-two in the New Town39. In subsequent years, the number of houses declined due to fires and war damage. The description of the city of 1749 mentions 263 plots, one hundred twenty-one of which remained vacant. In the census of 1772 there is information about only 136 houses situated within the city walls40. Four streets came off from the corners of the market, three of which led to the city gates. The major communication role was played by the eastwest route from the Gdańsk Gate to the Człuchów Gate, where the transit movement was concentrated. It was in front of the Gdańsk Gate that roads leading from the south (from Tuchola) and the northern track from Malbork and Gdańsk met. Behind the Człuchów Gate ran the road to the West to Człuchów. The Mill Gate was used mainly by the local traffic, for behind the gate there was the city’s village and the mill suburbs crossed by the road leading up to the city’s land estates and the city’s forest. After the establishment of the monastery of St. Augustine in the southern suburbs, the so called Monastic Gate was opened in the city walls which was designed for pedestrian traffic41. Probably a similar gate called “Paulsche Tor” was situated also in the northern part of the city walls at the mouth of Paulschergasse street42.

Chojnice, situated several kilometers from the frontier with Poland, played an important role in the defence system of the State of the Teutonic Order, which is why the construction of the fortifications started immediately after the establishment of the town. jan Długosz in his work “Annals or chronicles of the famous Kingdom of Poland” called Chojnice “the key and gate to Pomerania”. The first record about the fortifications and moat in the southern part comes from 1365. Apart from three gates, the city walls were reinforced with 23 wall towers, and from the west and south – with two moats and an earthen rampart. Access to the city was hindered from the north and east by natural obstacles such as lakes and marshes43. In the market square there were a town hall, butchers’ stalls and stallholders’ stands. According to the privilege of 1360 the Teutonic Order owned their own mansion in Chojnice, which was situated behind the parson’s house in the New Towns. The building was not a residence; it was occasionally visited by the commander of Człuchów when lands tribunals were held and rent was collected from the councils. Sometimes other officials and servants of the Teutonic Order who were passing through the city stayed in the mansion. The maintenance of the mansion was covered by rent paid by the city in corn and meat in return for the use of mills. In 1446 the Grand Master Konrad von Erlichshausen transferred perpetual usufruct of the mansion to the city44. As early as the Middle Ages in front of the city’s gates, suburbs started to develop. They originally played the role of an economic back area. From the west there were the Człuchów Suburbs with gardens and malt-house recorded in the 15th century45. West off the Człuchów Gate and the Mill Gate there was the city’s village, which hat their own mayor. This village was probably mentioned in the record of the 1470s referring to a settlement called Długa Wieś (Long Village) which was situated in the vicinity of the city of Chojnice near the mill. A wide route running from the south to the north in front of the Człuchów Gate, which is to be found in the city plans from the beginning of the 19th century, may be the remains of the spatial layout of the village. A village within the city and a small town on the territory of which it was created constituted one homogenous judicial-administrative area and one parish. In legal terms, the inhabitants of the village were burghers, while in economic terms they were peasants46. Industrial equipment, essential for the city’s economy, was to be found in the suburbs and the city’s fields. Behind the Mill Gate at jarcewo Stream, a mill recorded in the privilege of 1360 was erected. The second mill was located north of the city in the Dunkershagen manor. In 1377 the Grand Master allowed the city to construct two windmills in the city’s fields47. According to the description of 1749, in the Człuchów Suburbs and the Mill Suburbs apart from the above recorded mill there were several residential buildings, an inn, three distilleries, five malt-houses and 28 peasant’s stockyards48. The northern suburb with the city’s brickworks was less significant economically. Far from the city, next to the southern bank of Charzykowy Lake at jarcewo Stream, a tuck mill was built – this was used by clothiers from Chojnice49. Malt-houses, industrial buildings and gardens were recorded in the 15th century in the southern suburb developing in front of the Gdańsk Gate50. It was not until the early modern period that the residential role of suburbs grew significantly; while the source of 1570 mentioned only 4 houses located in the suburbs, the census of 1749 recorded 73 houses51.

The only indicator enabling us to estimate Chojnice’s population in the Middle Ages is the number of houses. Assuming that the average household consisted of 4–5 people, the city may have been inhabited by about 1000 people at the beginning of the 15th century. Probably the population of the city followed the general demographic trend in Prussia and decreased in the first half of the 15th century and during the Thirteen year War (1454–1466). The period of the demographic development commenced from the second half of the15th century and lasted until the beginning of the 17th century. On the basis of the data included in the description of the city of 1570 its population may be estimated at 1550 inhabitants52. In the 17th century the population declined by one third owing to the Swedish invasion and the epidemic of December 1657. In 1662 about 1100 people lived in Chojnice. Epidemics of 1705 and 1711 involved another decline in the population of the city. The demographic situation of the city started to improve in the mid18th century; in 1749 Chojnice was inhabited by 1250 people and in 1772 by 1588. Throughout the 17th and 18th centuries there took place a clear change in the proportion between the number of the inhabitants of the city and the suburbs. If in 1662 the suburbs were inhabited by 260 people, then in 1749 and 1772 their number rose to correspondingly 438 and 498 people. Irrespective of the demographic fluctuations, in the Middle Ages and in the early modern period Chojnice was the second most populated town in Pomerelia (after Gdańsk)53. After the Reformation in 1555 the majority of burghers were Evangelicals, the evidence of which is the fact that in the years 1661– –1772 only 33 Catholic inhabitants were granted town privileges. There were more Catholics among the poor who did not enjoy the city rights54. The privileged group were citizenspeople who owned full city rights. There was also the so-called grand citizenship which was connected with the right to brew beer. According to the census of 1772 Chojnice was inhabited by 129 citizens, 62 of whom enjoyed the grand citizenship. It is estimated that citizens constituted about one-third of all inhabitants. In the mid-18th century Chojnice became diversified in terms of social topography. Citizens lived mainly in houses situated within the city walls, while the poorer who did not have city rights resided in rented buildings in the suburbs55. In the years 1550–1770 almost 2070 people were registered in the citizens’ book, half of whom came from Chojnice and the vicinity. About 11% of citizens came from Gdańsk and smaller towns of Royal Prussia, 9% from Pomerania, 5% from Royal Prussia and 5% from Brandenburg. Relatively few new burghers (3%) moved to Chojnice from the Polish Kingdom. The German population prevailed among citizens – it was in German that the city books were written and the citizenship oath was taken56.

Craft was the most significant for the economy of the city in the Middle Ages and in the early modern period, for about two-thirds of inhabitants earned their living from artisanship. The dominant role of craft production is confirmed in the registers of inhabitants and the social-professional analysis of people upon whom the city rights had been confirmed in the 17th and 18th centuries – 86% of them were artisans, while representatives of professions connected with trade constituted merely 4,3%. Among the small towns of Pomerelia, Chojnice was the biggest centre of craft production. The census of 1570 enumerates 152 owners of workshops. Supposedly, the climax of the prosperous situation of Chojnice craft took place in the 1630s and 1640s. The damage caused by the wars of the mid-17th century and the beginning of the 18th century entailed a decrease in the number of craftsmen. In 1662 there were only 111 guild masters in the city, in 1749 – 115, and in 1772 – 12957. Medieval records mention representatives of several professions such as clothiers, bakers, butchers, tailors, brewers, linen draper, shoemakers, smiths, locksmiths, saddlers, cutlers, armourers58. In the early modern period the number of professions increased; the census of 1570 lists 19 professions, while the sources of the 17th and 18th centuries mention representatives of over 30 craft professions59. From the Middle Ages cloth-making was the most developed branch of craft. In 1348 and 1380 clothiers were granted privileges by the commander of Człuchów, thanks to which they were allowed to erect tuck mills at Charzykowy Lake. Two tuck mills were also mentioned in the early modern period60. Clothiers’ frames were to be found in the Gdańsk suburb. In Chojnice they produced grey cloth of relatively low quality for peasants and poorer inhabitants of cities. In the 16th and 17th centuries clothiers constituted almost one-third of all craftsmen – in the census of 1570 and 1662 there are recorded respectively 55 and 31 guild masters of this specialization61. In the 18th century cloth production decreased, as did the number of guild masters (10 in 1749 and 8 in 1772). Nevertheless, cloth-making and cloth trade were still considered the main pillar of the city’s economy62. The highest number of guilders were linen drapers (16 guild masters in 1570). However, in the second half of the 17th century the significance of linen-making declined markedly; the census of 1662 mentions only three linen drapers, while the census of 1749 only two. In the whole early modern period in Chojnice, professions connected with the production of clothes such as tailors and shoemakers were quite common. In the 18th century the decline in the production of fabrics was accompanied by the growing importance of food products, the most essential of which were bakery and brewery63. In Chojnice, beer was produced mainly for the local market. All owners of estates were allowed to make beer, whilst inhabitants of suburbs were deprived of this right. From the second half of the 17th century the significance of vodka production was gradually increasing so that in the 18th century the revenue from distillery exceeded the one from the production of beer. For safety reasons in 1696 the city council moved the distillery from the plots within the city walls to the Człuchów suburb64.

Chojnice never played a major role in long-distance trade as the city was situated away from the main trade routes; in the Middle Ages merchants travelling from Greater Poland to Gdańsk stopped in Chojnice sporadically65. The commercial significance of Chojnice was reduced to the local retail trade of food and craft products. It is estimated that inhabitants dealing with commerce constituted about 3% of the population. In the years 1550– –1770 thirty-seven merchants and twenty-one representatives of professions connected with retail trade (pharmacists, stallholders, vendors) were given city rights, which constituted about 3 % of all people registered in the citizens’ book. Retail trade was concentrated in the market square and in stalls situated next to the town hall. The basic form of trade contacts with local peasants were weekly fairs66. Foreign merchants arrived in Chojnice a few times a year to take part in fairs. The first information about a fair comes from 1420. In 1472, the right to organize a second fair granted city the King Casimir IV. In the 17th century there took place one summer fair (24 june) and two autumn fairs (29 Sept and 29 Oct) in Chojnice67. Besides, there were special fairs where only cloth, wool and linen were sold (twice a year) and recurrent fairs thanks to which the city was supplied with basic alimentary products (flour, grain, meat). In the 17th century Chojnice became one of the most important centres for the purchase of grain in the southern part of Pomerelia. Merchants also sold local fabrics which they exported to Gdańsk and Grudziądz68. As opposed to other small towns in Royal Prussia, agriculture played a relatively minor role in the economic life of Chojnice. In the 16th and 17th centuries about 8% of people were involved in agriculture. The process of agrarianisation became more intense during the crisis of craft production in the first half of the 18th century when the percentage of peasants increased to 12%. Most lands in the area of the landed patrimony (about 2130 ha) were utilised by peasants who lived in the city’s village situated in front of the Człuchów Gate. In part of the city’s estates there were located two manors (Giegel, Hilfe) belonging to the city council. Horses, cattle, sheep and pigs belonging to burghers were grazed on pastures located in the area of the city’s patrimony. According to the data of 1772 inhabitants of Chojnice bred 153 horses, 242 units of cattle and 591 units of sheep. The city council also received revenues from the lease of three mills, two windmills, a brickworks and a limestone quarry69.

In the Middle Ages the church structures in the south-west part of Pomerelia were part of the Pomeranian archdeaconry supervised by the Archbishop of Gniezno. On the strength of the decision of the archbishop jan Łaski in 1512 the Pomeranian archdeaconry was incorporated into the archdeaconry of Kamień (Cammin). The parish was probably created when the city was founded, but it was mentioned for the first time in the privilege of 1360, in which the Teutonic Order granted the parson 6 lans of land. The first record about the parish church of St. john the Baptist comes from 1365. Between the church and the city walls stood the parson’s house. The Grand Master had the right of patronage over the parish; he appointed fellow priests from the Teutonic Order for the position of parson. After 1466 the King of Poland took over the right to present candidates to the position of parson. From the end of the 14th century the parson of Chojnice also played the function of a dean who supervised 19 adjacent parishes70. Chojnice was one of the few small Prussian towns which in the Middle Ages possessed an extended sacral topography. In 1356 the Grand Master Winrich von Kniprode granted to the monastery of St. Augustine part of the island situated south of the city walls, and gave permission for the construction of monastic buildings and a church of the Holy Cross. Monks were also given the right to collect alms in the city71. At the turn of the 15th and 16th centuries the Chojnice monastery, like convents of other mendicant orders in Prussian towns, faced a serious crisis; the number of monks was declining, as was their influence among the burghers. In 1518 the last monks left Chojnice, and in 1534 the dilapidated monastic buildings were taken over by the city council and designated for demolition. In 1624 on the strength of the royal sentence the order of St. Augustine made an attempt to reconstruct their convent in Chojnice, but the fire in 1655 scuppered their plans. After the Polish-Swedish war terminated (1660), monks returned to Chojnice and reconstructed the church and monastic buildings72.

Beyond the city walls, two hospitals were built in the Middle Ages. In the Gdańsk suburbs, in the main road leading to the city from the southern side there was a chapel and hospital of St. George where people suffering from leprosy found shelter. Originally, the right of patronage over the chapel which was first recorded in 1384 belonged to the Teutonic Order, but in the 15th century the city council took over the administration of the hospital [in 1457 lay administrators of St. George were recorded]37. After leprosy disappeared in Prussia in the 15th century, the hospital provided shelter for the poor. In 1619 seven and in 1653 eleven residents lived there73. In the second half of the 14th century the Teutonic Order set up a hospital of the Holy Spirit in the western suburb near the road leading to Człuchów. In 1555 both hospitals were taken over by the Protestant community. The shelter of St. George returned to the Catholics in 1618, but it eventually ceased to exist after the fire of 165674. In the second quarter of the 16th century Martin Luther’s teachings were becoming more and more popular in Chojnice. They were brought by peripatetic preachers and young men who studied at universities in Germany. The city council headed by the mayor Michael jöde supported the Reformation. In 1555 the privilege of King Sigismund August granting Chojnice religious freedom allowed the Lutherans to take over the parish church and hospital chapels. The majority of burghers converted to Lutheranism; in consequence, Catholicism became marginalised75. After leaving the parish church of St. john the Baptist the Catholic parson held services in a village church in Powałki ( 10 km north-east of Chojnice) which was situated within the Chojnice parish. At the end of the 16th century, archbishops of Gniezno and parsons of Chojnice applied to the royal court to regain churches and property taken over by Protestants. On the strength of the court’s verdict of 1613 and the settlement concluded between the city council and the parson jan Gleissen Doręgowski in 1616 Lutherans returned the parish church and the chapel and hospital of St. George to the Catholics, while the hospital and chapel of the Holy Spirit remained in their hands. In 1620 the city council allowed Protestant masses to be held in the upper part of the town hall, and in 1623 the whole building was converted into the church of the Holy Trinity. At the same time a new town hall was erected for the city council in the market square76.

Having regained the parish church, the parson of Chojnice managed to get the support of the jesuits. The first jesuits arrived in Chojnice in 1620. Thanks to bestowments from the Catholic clergy and the Polish nobility, monks built their own residence with a school near the parish church. In 1664 the first wooden church was erected; after the fire of 1712 the construction of a brick church of the Annunciation to the Blessed Virgin Mary started. The construction of the church finished in 1744. The extension of the convent allowed the jesuits to take over the former City Court in 1743, where in the years 1744–1755 a new building of the college was erected77. As early as 1375 in Chojnice a parish school was established. Its history was closely linked with the history of the parish. In 1555 it was taken over by the Protestants, and in 1618 it went back being a Catholic parish78. After 1627 a new school building was built; it also included flats for a teacher and church servants. In 1617 the city council set up an Evangelical city school which was located in Staroszkolna street. From 1623 the jesuits ran a Catholic school, which in 1630, on the strength of the royal privilege, was turned into a college – an institution of secondary education79. As a result of the second partition of Poland, Chojnice was situated within the borders of the Prussian Kingdom; on 21 Sept 1772 the Prussian army marched into the city and three days later on 27 Sept the city’s mayor and councillors took an oath of allegiance to King Frederic II in Malbork. After Prussia had been defeated in the war with Napoleon in 1806, Chojnice was occupied by the Polish troops supporting the French army. The Polish rule lasted only a few months as the peace treaty of Tilsit (1807) returned Pomerelia under Prussian rule. During Napoleon’s expedition to Russia (1812–1813), the inhabitants of Chojnice were forced to pay the French army a war contribution, which heavily affected the city’s budget. The Congress of Vienna of 1815 stipulated that Prussia maintain its rule over Pomerelia80. The long period of peace was interrupted by the outbreak of WWI in 1914. Chojnice was not directly involved in military procedures. Inhabitants of the city were affected by the effects of the fights in East Prussia in 1914 when a hospital for injured and sick soldiers was set up in Chojnice. According to the decisions made at the peace conference in Versailles, Pomerelia was reunited with Poland. The Weimar Republic acknowledged the Treaty of Versailles of 10 january 1920; the Polish administration gained authority over Chojnice on 31 january 192081.

Having seized Chojnice, the Prussian authorities did away with the old self-governing political system; the administrative and judicial powers were given to officials appointed by the state, the police mayor and the judicial mayor. In 1808 a new regulation reintroduced the institution of the city council elected by citizens. There were 155 people eligible for voting in 1809. The council elected the administrative authorities which consisted of a mayor, treasury administrator and a magistrate consisting of 3–6 officials. The choice had to be approved of by the state authorities. The judiciary was excluded from the city’s local authority and was now supervised by the state82. The power of the city’s administrative bodies extended also to landed estates where, as in the early modern period, there were two manors, peasants’ farms, mills and the city’s forest. According to a new election law introduced in 1853, citizens eligible for voting were divided into three groups (curias) depending on the amount of tax they paid. The system guaranteed that the wealthiestmerchants, entrepreneurs, representatives of the intelligentsia and land owners – should always prevail in the city council83. In the Prussian state Chojnice kept its status as a district town. In 1772 the boundaries of the Chojnice district included the southern part of Pomerelia. In 1818 the district’s area was reduced as new districts were created in Świecie and Człuchów. In 1875 a separate district of Tuchola was created from the southern part of the Chojnice district. The district was headed by a district administrator – Landrat – appointed by the state authorities84. In Chojnice apart from officials of the municipal and district authorities there were also judicial offices. From 1815 a landed tribunal and municipal tribunal (Landund Stadtgericht) were in operation. In 1849 municipal and district courts were introduced, while in 1879 a regional court (Amtsgericht) was set up, as was another court the authority of which extended to adjacent districts in Człuchów, Złotów and Tuchola85. The medieval spatial layout was preserved in Chojnice until the mid-19th century. The city plan of 1822 shows well-maintained city walls with fortified towers and gates. Along the city walls ran a moat, and from the southern side there was a defensive rampart where a rope-making factory was in operation. Only the western part of the city walls was demolished between 1810 and 1822. Houses within the city walls were made mainly of brick, but the majority of buildings had wooden porches which survived until the beginning of the 20th century – the time when they were abolished for safety reasons. A new element in the land development in the city was a building of a barracks constructed in the years 1786–1787 (extended in 1866) in

the north-west part of the New Town next to the city walls. In the 1820s burghers started to demolish the medieval walls gradually in order to get building material. In the suburbs thatched wooden houses prevailed; their architecture resembled Kashubian cottages86. As a result of the growing settlement in the suburbs the number of houses increased, with the fast growth occurring in the first years of the Prussian rule. Between 1772 and 1778 the number of buildings grew from 195 to 236, but only 84 houses had tiled roofs. In 1825 the number of residential buildings went up to 319, and in 1852 to 374. A dynamic development took place in the second half of the 19th century. In 1871 in Chojnice there were 440 houses and in 1905 – 57187. In the first half of the 19th century the Człuchów suburb maintained its agricultural character – the area was occupied mainly by peasants’ farms. A settlement of linen drapers brought to Chojnice by Frederic II was established between present Plac jagielloński (Denkmals-Platz) and Człuchowska street (Schlochauerstraβe) in the 1780s. In the 1840s buildings between Plac jagielloński (Denkmals-Platz) and Strzelecka (Schützenstraβe) and Pietruszkowa (Petersilienstraβe) streets were destroyed by fire. In the Gdańsk suburb there prevailed buildings designed for the purposes of commerce and craft such as breweries, barns and granaries belonging to burghers along with houses and workshops of clothiers. In the eastern outskirts of the suburb there was a cemetery of the Evangelical community and a Catholic cemetery88. The extension and modernisation of the urban planning in the second half of the 19th century was a consequence of the growing number of inhabitants and the increasing significance of Chojnice as a road and rail hub. In 1829 a road from Berlin to Königsberg was supplied to the city. In 1847 a road to Bytów was built. In 1856 a road to Nakło – an important transshipment point of agricultural products – was constructed. At the same time the laying of new roads to Tuchola and Brusy was undertaken. In 1871 a railroad between Piła and Tczew was launched; it connected Chojnice with the most important rail roads to Berlin and Gdańsk. In subsequent years further rail connections were opened: to Człuchów (1877), Laskowice ((1883), Nakło (1894), and Lipusz in Kashubia (1902)89. New traffic conditions determined the development of a new district in the former Gdańsk suburb. The centre of the district was Wilhelm’s Square – Wilhelms-Platz (presently Plac Niepodległości). On the northern side of the square a complex of buildings of St. Bartholomew’s hospital was erected in 1886-8790. From the square ran a new street – Bahnhofstraβe leading up to the railway station (at present Piłsudski street and Dworcowa street) along which mainly villas were built. The Housing Cooperative of Office Workers started building houses in Warszawska street (Bismarkstraβe) which was a branch of Dworcowa street. At the eastern end of the suburb, behind the Evangelical cemetery a district hospital was erected in the years 1914–1917 (at present in Żwirki i Wigury street)91. Throughout the 19th century a new district developed between the city and Zakonne Lake. In the early modern period the monastery of St. Augustine was the most important building in the area, but in 1819 it was taken over by the state and converted into a dormitory for students of the gymnasium school. At the beginning of the 19th century a synagogue was built near the monastery at the corner of Bankowa street and Sukienników street (Conviktand Rähme-Straβe). The main traffic artery of this part of the city became Sukienników street (Rähmestraβe), constructed on the spot of the former defensive rampart which enabled the communication from the east to the west not entering the Old Town. In 1862 on the southern side of the street a municipal hospital was built. The layout of streets remained unchanged in the Człuchów suburb except the wide road leading to the city’s village which was turned into two public squares. On the spot of the pond Denkmal-Platz was built (at present Plac jagielloński), the name of which refers to the monument erected in 1881 which commemorated the inhabitants of Chojnice who had died during the French-Prussian war (1870–1871)92. In the southern part of the former village, Königs-Platz ( was built; it played an important role in the city’s communication as roads to Nakło, Bytów and Człuchów ran from it. At the beginning of the 20th century Człuchowska street and Strzelecka street were changed into wide promenades leading up to the park and the shooting manor built in the years 1785–1788. Buildings of administrative and judicial institutions constructed in the second half of the 19th century gave a new image to the Człuchów suburb. At the end of the axis of Człuchowska street there was a building where the district authorities resided (1892). In front of the former Mill Gate (demolished in 1836) a complex of judicial buildings (1879) and a jail (1865) were constructed93. In the vicinity of the church and the poorhouse of the Holy Spirit a complex of buildings dedicated to the primary school for boys was established in 1861 and extended in 1909; the school for girls received a new building in 188294. The Old Town was also modernised. In the 1880s the awareness of the need to protect monuments was strong enough to allow the preservation of the Człuchów Gate – a passageway was broadened to make the traffic go smoothly through it. The biggest changes were introduced in the market square. After the old town hall and the guardhouse at the church of the Holy Trinity were demolished, a new building was erected for the local administration next to the northern frontage (1901–1902). In the western part of the market an imposing building of the post office was constructed (1886)95. Areas north of the Old Town did not develop so intensively. Residential buildings were erected only along Ziegelstraβe (at present Mickiewicza street) and Hohe Höfe (at present Wysoka street). In the fields north of Cegielniane Lake a jewish cemetery and a municipal slaughterhouse were set up. On the

site of the former municipal farm Giegel a youth detention centre (1885) and an estate for homeless farm workers (1892) were built96. Cegielniane Lake which, like Zakonne Lake, was situated in the southern part and only accumulated the city’s sewage and so hindered the development of the residential or industrial infrastructure in this part of the city. After the great epidemic of cholera in 1866 the decision was made to drain and cover Cegielniane Lake. In 1886 a canal was built, which allowed channeling water from Zakonne Lake97. At the beginning of the 20th century the most important municipal facilities were built in Chojnice such as a gas company, waterworks and power station in 1900 along with the sewerage system in 190998. In the last quarter of the 18th century, Chojnice flourished in terms of demography and economy. In 1786 thirty-six families from German countries settled in Chojnice having received substantial assistance from the Prussian authorities. As a result of the influx of new settlers, the number of inhabitants in the period up to the outbreak of the Napoleonic wars increased by almost 20% (from 1588 to 1876)99. The demographic boom was not hindered by epidemics of cholera of 1831, 1848/1849 and 1866. In the first half of the 19th century, the number of inhabitants grew to 5029 (in 1855) only to double in the second half of the 19th century. According to the census of 1910, 11 980 people lived in Chojnice100. Owing to the 19th century influx of Catholics from adjacent villages, the religious structure of the population had changed. The percentage of Catholics rose from 27% in 1821 to 53% in 1910, while the number of Evangelicals declined from 70% to 45%. The religious structure to a large extent overlapped with the social and financial structure. Catholics prevailed among the working class and the poorer strata of the society, whilst representatives of the upper and middle classes (merchants, officials, entrepreneurs) were mostly Evangelicals. Until 1920 it was the German population that constituted the majority in the city. At the beginning of the 20th century, Poles constituted a mere 7% of those living in Chojnice. From the end of the 18th century, jewish traders started to settle in Chojnice. According to the census of 1816, the jewish community consisted of 44 people. The size of the community continued to grow until the 1880s when 563 jews lived in Chojnice – 5.6% of the entire population. In subsequent years, the number of jews diminished considerably owing to emigration. According to the census of 1910, jews constituted only 2% of the whole population (257 persons)101. A brick synagogue was erected in about 1830 at Zakonne Lake, on the corner of the streets Konviktstrasses and Rähmestrasse (at present Bankowa street and Sukienników street). The oldest jewish cemetery was situated in the northern part of the city, at the crossing of the streets Ziegel and Lämmer-strasse (at present Mickiewicza street and Zielona street). In 1900 a new jewish cemetery was established in the vicinity (in Hohe Höfe street – at present Wysoka street)102.

When Chojnice was incorporated into Prussia in 1772, the most important role was played by the trade of corn and weaving. The Prussian authorities intended to revive the craft of drapery; with this aim they financed the redecoration of the tuck mill and the construction of two dye-works. Public resources were also used to build a plant producing linen. Nevertheless, the dynamic development of textile craft lasted for a short time. Most weaving workshops went bankrupt after Chojnice had lost access to the Russian and Polish markets and had to face competition from German countries103. Craft constituted the basis for the economic existence of Chojnice until the outbreak of WWI. The industrial revolution did not affect the city’s development – at the beginning of the 20th century, 266 craft workshops were in operation, while only 200 people were employed in the industrial sector. The biggest industrial plant – the machine factory of Bruno Riedel – employed about 40 workers. Until the beginning of the 20th century, the city still played a major role in the wholesale trade of crops104. When the city belonged to Poland in the years 1920–1939, it maintained the status of an important centre for local and state administration. The political system of Chojnice did not differ significantly from that of the Prussian period. The most important body of the local authorities was the city council consisting of 30 members elected by the city’s inhabitants. It appointed the mayor of the city and five members of the magistrate. In Chojnice there were also offices of the district administration – the starost and the District Dietine, along with the grodzki court (court of first instance), the district court and a jail. The city’s location 2 kilometres from the PolishGerman border enabled the establishment of the Inspectorate of the Border Guards, customs offices, and the First Riffle Battalion in Chojnice with new barracks built in Świętopelka street in 1936105. In the interwar period, the city’s population increased by 55% – from 10,435 in 1921 to 16, 213 in 1937. As a result of the emigration of Germans and jews, the ethnic profile of the city changed considerably. In 1937 Germans constituted only 12% of the population, while the jews merely 0.3%106. What distinguished Chojnice from other Pomeranian towns was the large number of inhabitants employed in institutions of state or local authorities, which was the consequence of the fact that the city was a major administrative centre. According to the data of 1931, this group constituted 47% of the whole population. 17% of Chojnice’s inhabitants were employed in industry and craft, while 9% in trade107.

In the years 1920–1939 the city centre maintained its former image. The only significant change was the demolition of the church of the Holy Spirit situated in front of the Człuchów Gate in 1938. The areas situated between the Old Town and the railway station along with the main street exits were the place where most residential buildings were constructed. In the 1930s between Piłsudskiego street and Gdańska street, a new network of streets was demarcated (i.e. Żwirki i Wigury, Sambora, Mestwina, Subisława streets), where the construction of new houses was undertaken with flats mainly for office workers and members of the intelligentsia. A new phenomenon was the existence of housing cooperatives which erected single-family houses for the working class. In the years 1928–1934 almost 70 houses for workers were built in Bytowska street; a few years later similar houses were constructed between Bytowska and Strzelecka streets (Polesie street) and in Gdańska street. In order to improve the living conditions of the working class, two complexes of allotments were built in the 1930s in Żwirki i Wigury street and in Bytowska street. In the 1930s the local authorities were increasingly concerned about the development of some areas of former municipal lakes. In 1932 on the site of the dried Cegielniane Lake, a municipal stadium was constructed, while a municipal park was set up around the pond which remained after Zakonne Lake108. On 1 September 1939 Chojnice was occupied by the German army. The city’s architecture was not damaged during the brief combat. It was not until the first months of the Nazi occupation that the synagogue was burnt down and the Church of the Holy Trinity was demolished. The Nazis murdered the jewish population and a great number (155 persons) of the members of the Polish intelligentsia and social activists109. Within the project of the construction of the road from Berlin to Königsberg the main west-east artery of the city leading through Człuchowska, Sukienników and Gdańska streets was built. The Nazi authorities continued the project of erecting multi-family houses in the borough situated between Gdańska street and the railway station (at present Żwirki i Wigury, Drzymały, Mestwina streets). Several multi-family houses were also built in Człuchowska street110.

On 14 February 1945 the Soviet army liberated Chojnice after a few days of fighting. As a result of military activity and arson committed after the city had been conquered, about 60% of buildings in the city centre were demolished. Only the northern frontage with the town hall survived in the market square111. In the political system of real socialism the local authorities were answerable to the state authorities and the party. From 1945 the district of Chojnice belonged to the Bydgoszcz province, and in 1999 it was incorporated into the Pomeranian Province. After 1945 the city’s population grew rapidly. In 1945 Chojnice had 12,444 inhabitants, while twenty years later the population rose to 22,622 in 1980, in 1980 to 31,995, and in 2013 to 40, 306112. In the first quarter of the post-war period the demographic development did not go hand in hand with urban and economic development. Until the 1960s new buildings were constructed only in the Old Town on the sites of buildings demolished in 1945, and in the boroughs created at the end of the 19th century and in the first decades of the 20th century – from the west in front of the former Człuchów Gate (Człuchowska street, january 31 street) and near the railway station (Drzymały street, Łanowa street). At the beginning of the 1970s the Housing Co-operative launched the construction of new residential estates (Świętopełka estate and Budowlanych estate) in the south-east part of Chojnice between Warszawska street and Gdańska street. The intensive development of the residential building sector in new and hitherto undeveloped areas started in the mid 1970s. It was then that the estates of Osiedle Hallera and Osiedle 700-lecia were built. They were concrete prefabricated housing projects devoid of any individual features, which was typical of the socialist house building sector. Single-family houses were built at that time in the areas situated in the southwest and northern parts of the city. The development of new estates in the 1970s was connected with the establishment of large machinery and metal industrial plants in Chojnice. The growing industrialisation of the city led to the creation of a new industrial estate between Lichnowska street and Tucholska street113.

The social and urban development of the city in the second half of the 20th century did not entail the enlargement of the city’s area, for on the strength of the decisions of the state authorities of 1949 and 1968 the municipality was deprived of forests and the countryside which had belonged to it since the Middle Ages. Hence, the municipality’s area was reduced from 3086 hectares in 1939 to 2066 hectares in 1968.
